hook: Fifteen products, one decision matrix. Pick by **constraints**, not by hype.

scenes.title: pgvector: the **boring-correct** default
scenes.sub: Postgres you already run — now with vectors
scenes.narration: You met pgvector in Reel 24; here's its competitive position. Strengths: zero new infrastructure — the database you already operate, back up, and secure; transactional consistency between vectors and metadata; SQL joins for hybrid queries; honest scale to millions of vectors per node. Weaknesses: not a dedicated ANN engine — throughput and index efficiency lag specialized stores at tens of millions of vectors; HNSW in Postgres is memory-hungry. Verdict: the default for applications, prototypes, and multi-tenant systems up to moderate scale. Graduate when measurements — not marketing — say so.

items.s: Existing Postgres estate · moderate scale · strong consistency + filter needs
Memory footprint of HNSW; vacuum/analyze habits change with vector indexes
Millions of vectors and thousands of QPS → still fine; tens of millions + sustained heavy load → benchmark dedicated stores

scenes.narration: pgvector's decision card. It wins on operational consolidation — one system, one backup, one auth model — and on queries that mix similarity with relational business logic, which is most of them in business software. The watch-outs are operational: HNSW indexes want RAM, and vector-heavy tables change Postgres tuning habits — revisit autovacuum and memory settings. Set a measurement-triggered exit: define the latency and throughput SLA, benchmark, and let numbers — not architecture fashion — pick the moment to move.

scenes.title: Azure AI Search: enterprise **with a compliance badge**
scenes.narration: For the Microsoft estate — and your Deloitte context, this matters — Azure AI Search is the managed vector-plus-keyword search with enterprise plumbing: private endpoints, Entra ID auth, regional data residency, and SLAs. It does hybrid search natively — BM25 and vectors with fusion — plus AI enrichment pipelines that chunk and embed during ingestion. Trade-offs: Azure-shaped pricing that rewards understanding it; query-model details that differ from the open-source stores; and the usual managed-service trade — less control, less operational burden. When the client's security review demands Microsoft-managed everything, this is your vector layer.

items.s: Azure-native estates · compliance-driven clients · hybrid search without assembly
Private networking, Entra auth, DI-based ingestion — enterprise checklist, pre-ticked
SKU + capacity units — cheaper at steady load than bursty dev; model it before committing

scenes.narration: The enterprise calculus. Azure AI Search shines when the surrounding estate is Azure and the security questionnaire is long — the managed integration deletes whole sections of it. Hybrid retrieval and semantic ranking come assembled rather than built. The honest caveats: pricing rewards predictable capacity, so dev environments can feel expensive; and as with any managed service, you trade fine-grained control for operational peace. In client architecture conversations, it's the answer that keeps procurement, security, and the roadmap all smiling — price it honestly and it's frequently the right call.

scenes.title: Qdrant, Chroma, FAISS — the **self-host spectrum**
scenes.sub: From embedded library to production server
scenes.narration: The open-source tier spans three shapes. FAISS is a library — not a database: the fastest raw ANN indexes, no server, no persistence, no metadata queries; you build everything around it. Chroma is the embedded-friendly store — pip install, runs in-process like DuckDB, perfect for prototypes and small apps. Qdrant is the full production server — HNSW with filtering done right, payload indexes, replication, a real ops story; self-host it on your VMs or their cloud. The pattern mirrors your DuckDB journey: FAISS is a library, Chroma is embedded, Qdrant is the server. Choose per scale and ops appetite.

items.s: Benchmark-winning indexes in-process; you own persistence + metadata
Zero-ops vector DB in your app process — prototypes and small production
Filtering-friendly HNSW, replication, snapshots — the open-source workhorse

scenes.narration: Positioning the trio. FAISS when you're building an engine, not an application — the speed king, the flexibility king, the responsibility king. Chroma when you want a database-feel with library-feel operations — the demo-to-small-prod sweet spot. Qdrant when self-hosting is a requirement and production characteristics matter — filtering at scale, replication, backups. All three speak the same mental model from GA-09 — collections, vectors, payloads, k-NN — so prototyping in Chroma and graduating to Qdrant is nearly free. The lock-in risk here is pleasantly low.

scenes.title: Pinecone & friends: **pay, don't operate**
scenes.sub: The SaaS trade: zero ops, ongoing rent, data leaves your VPC
scenes.narration: Pinecone defined the managed vector category: serverless indexing, no shards to babysit, scaling without capacity planning. The deal is pure SaaS: you pay per usage and per storage, forever; your data transits a vendor's cloud; and the lock-in is real — not from file formats, but from operational habits and API shapes. When to say yes: small teams shipping fast, spiky workloads, no ops capacity, proofs of concept that must impress. When to negotiate hard: enterprise data residency requirements, steady high-volume workloads where self-host math wins after the first year, and clients who count vendors as risk.

items.s: Speed to market · variable load · no platform team · demo-grade reliability
Steady load: compare 1yr SaaS spend vs self-host VMs + eng time — often a crossover
Enterprise clients may simply rule SaaS out — know before you propose

scenes.narration: The SaaS decision framework. Say yes when velocity and variable scale dominate — startups, spikes, small teams. Run the crossover math for steady-state enterprise load: a year of SaaS invoices versus a couple of VMs plus fractional ops time; the self-host line usually wins beyond it. And lead with the constraint nobody can negotiate: where is the data ALLOWED to live? For regulated clients that answer deletes the SaaS column before the demo starts. Presenting all three postures — pgvector, self-hosted Qdrant, managed Pinecone — with honest math is exactly the architect-level consulting this course trains you for.

scenes.title: Your relational DB wants vectors **too**
scenes.sub: SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL — verify current support; it's 2026
scenes.narration: The incumbents aren't sitting still. Vector capabilities have been landing in the relational databases enterprises already own — SQL Server added vector functions and index support in recent releases, Oracle has had vector search, others are following. Verify the CURRENT state — this space moved monthly — but the strategic meaning is stable: for clients with strict consolidation mandates, 'vectors in the database we already license' may beat every other option on procurement alone. The technical bar to check: index type and recall characteristics, dimension limits, and whether filtering performance meets your SLA at your scale.

items.s: Version-specific: check docs for your client's EXACT SQL Server/Oracle version
Which ANN structure, recall at your scale, behavior under heavy filtering
'Already licensed' beats 'new vendor' in many enterprise rooms — use it

scenes.narration: The verification discipline. These features land per-version and per-edition, and fast-moving docs mean last quarter's 'no' is this quarter's 'yes' — verify against the exact versions in the client's estate. Technically, interrogate the ANN index: what algorithm, what recall at your million-vector scale, what happens to latency when filters are selective. And politically: in enterprise architecture rooms, 'the capability we already own' carries enormous weight — when it clears your technical bar, it's often the recommendation that actually ships.

scenes.title: Score against **your** constraints
scenes.sub: Scale, ops, security, cost — four columns, honest numbers
scenes.narration: The selection matrix, in one breath. Scale: pgvector to millions per node; Qdrant and Pinecone to hundreds of millions; FAISS to billions if you build the shell. Ops: SaaS is zero, pgvector inherits your existing ops, Qdrant is a new server to run. Security: pgvector and self-hosted keep data in your perimeter; SaaS and cloud-managed trade perimeter for convenience. Cost: steady-state self-host usually wins past year one; bursty and early-stage favors SaaS. Run the matrix per client, document the decision — the next reel makes the chosen store stay healthy in production.

items.s: Recall + latency + filtered QPS on your vectors — synthetic benchmarks lie politely
Architecture Decision Record: options, scores, the call, the review trigger
Abstract behind your retrieval interface; vectors + IDs migrate — habits don't

scenes.narration: The process that makes the matrix real. Benchmark with your own vectors and query mix — every vendor's demo is beautiful. Record the decision as an ADR — options considered, numbers, the chosen path, and the trigger that reopens it. And engineer the exit: a thin retrieval interface in your code means the store is a replaceable detail; your vectors and metadata migrate mechanically. You're not buying a vector database forever — you're renting one until the constraints change. Design like you know it.

scenes.title: Chosen? Now keep it healthy
scenes.next: Reel 27 · Operations — upserts, sizing, multi-tenancy, backup & DR

recap: pgvector = consolidation default; Azure AI Search = Microsoft-estate enterprise; Qdrant/Chroma/FAISS = self-host spectrum; Pinecone = SaaS velocity
Relational DBs are adding vectors — verify per-version before proposing
Benchmark your corpus, write the ADR, keep the exit open via a thin retrieval interface

quiz.q: A client's estate is pure Azure and security review demands Microsoft-managed services. Strongest vector-store fit?
quiz.why: Managed, Entra-integrated, hybrid-capable, with the compliance posture an Azure-native client requires — the enterprise checklist comes pre-ticked.

quiz.q: When does self-hosting (e.g. Qdrant) usually beat SaaS (e.g. Pinecone) on cost?
opts: Steady, high-volume workloads beyond the ~12-month crossover point
quiz.why: Variable/bursty load favors SaaS; steady enterprise load usually crosses over when a year of invoices exceeds VMs + fractional ops time.

quiz.q: What's the best protection against vector-store lock-in?
opts: A thin retrieval interface in your code + portable vectors/metadata + an ADR with a review trigger
quiz.why: Vectors and metadata migrate mechanically; what locks you in is scattered API calls. Abstract the interface and the store becomes a replaceable detail.

code.title: The thin retrieval interface — swap stores without tears
code.body:
from typing import Protocol, Any

class Hit(BaseModel):
    id: str
    score: float
    payload: dict

class Retriever(Protocol):
    def upsert(self, ids: list[str], vecs, payloads: list[dict]) -> None: ...
    def search(self, vec, k: int = 10, where: dict | None = None) -> list[Hit]: ...
    def delete(self, ids: list[str]) -> None: ...

# --- one implementation per store ---------------------------------
class QdrantRetriever:
    def __init__(self, client, collection: str):
        self.c, self.col = client, collection
    def search(self, vec, k=10, where=None):
        r = self.c.search(self.col, vec, limit=k,
                          query_filter=self._f(where) if where else None)
        return [Hit(id=h.id, score=h.score, payload=h.payload) for h in r]

class PgvectorRetriever:
    def __init__(self, engine): self.engine = engine
    def search(self, vec, k=10, where=None):
        sql = text("""SELECT id, 1-(embedding <=> :q) AS score, payload
                      FROM docs
                      WHERE (:tenant IS NULL OR tenant_id = :tenant)
                      ORDER BY embedding <=> :q LIMIT :k""")
        ...  # same Hit shape

# --- app code depends on the Protocol, never a store --------------
def answer_question(q: str, retriever: Retriever):
    hits = retriever.search(embed(q), k=5, where={"tenant": current_tenant()})
    return generate(context=[h.payload["text"] for h in hits])
# Qdrant today, pgvector for a conservative client, Azure next —
# the app doesn't change.
annot: Protocol again (PY-05): structural typing — any store with these 3 methods qualifies
Hit is the one portable shape: id + score + payload
New store = one new Retriever class; zero changes to application code

notes:
# Vector DB Options

## pgvector
- Postgres + vectors. Default for apps/prototypes/multi-tenant to millions of vectors.
- Watch: HNSW memory, vacuum habits. Exit when measurements demand.

## Azure AI Search
- Managed, Entra-integrated, hybrid + semantic ranking, AI enrichment.
- Wins: Azure estates, compliance-driven clients. Model SKU/capacity pricing.

## Open-source spectrum
- **FAISS**: library (indexes only — you build the DB).
- **Chroma**: embedded, zero-ops — prototypes → small prod.
- **Qdrant**: self-hosted production server — filtering-friendly HNSW, replication.

## Pinecone & managed SaaS
- Zero ops, serverless scaling, ongoing rent, data leaves your VPC.
- 12-month crossover math decides vs self-host.

## Relational built-ins
- SQL Server / Oracle / others adding vector search — **verify per exact version**.
- 'Already licensed' wins procurement rooms when it clears the technical bar.

## Selection matrix
- Score: scale · ops · security/data-residency · cost (steady-state math).
- Benchmark YOUR corpus (recall + filtered QPS) · write the ADR · keep a thin Retriever interface so the store is replaceable.
